title: Data Communication and Computer Networks
description: The Internet from the application down to the wire: what each layer does, how packets get from your laptop to a server, how to compute delay and throughput, and how the link, wireless, multimedia, security and management pieces fit. Built week by week against the SZABIST outline.
textbook: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (6th ed). Forouzan and Stallings for numericals and physical-layer detail.

modules.title: Networks, protocols, and why we layer
modules.outline: Introduction to communication and networks, the Internet, the network edge. Why protocols and algorithms matter. The necessity of layered architecture.

lessons.title: What the Internet actually is
lessons.objective: describe the Internet in nuts-and-bolts terms and in service terms, and define a protocol precisely enough for an exam.

lessons.title: The network edge and how you get on it
lessons.objective: classify access networks by medium, sharing and rate, and explain when a neighbour can slow you down.

lessons.title: Why layers, and the two models you must know
lessons.objective: justify layered architecture, name the OSI and TCP/IP layers with their PDUs, and say which devices implement which layers.

lessons.title: Week 1 checkpoint
lessons.objective: answer exam-style questions on week 1 without notes.

modules.title: The network core: switching and performance
modules.outline: OSI and TCP/IP layers, the network core, circuit switching versus packet switching, and performance metrics: delay, loss, throughput.

lessons.title: Circuit switching vs packet switching
lessons.objective: compare the two switching approaches, compute what FDM and TDM circuits give you, and explain statistical multiplexing with numbers.

lessons.title: The four delays
lessons.objective: compute processing, queueing, transmission and propagation delay, and end-to-end delay across N store-and-forward links.

lessons.title: Throughput, loss, and reading a traceroute
lessons.objective: find the bottleneck link, explain why packets get dropped, and read a traceroute like a network engineer.

lessons.title: Week 2 checkpoint
lessons.objective: solve the numericals and comparison questions the midterm will draw from weeks 1 and 2.

lessons.title: Quiz 1 revision
lessons.objective: drill lectures 01 to 04 in quiz format before quiz 1 on Tuesday 29 September: definitions, layer jobs, switching, and delay and throughput numericals.

modules.title: Network types and transmission media
modules.outline: LAN, MAN, WAN and low-power WAN. IoT and the future of networks. Wired and wireless communication media.

lessons.title: PAN to WAN, peer-to-peer to client-server
lessons.objective: classify a network by the area it spans and by the role its machines play, and reproduce the lecture's LAN, MAN, WAN comparison while knowing which of its rows are wrong.

lessons.title: Topologies: bus, star, ring, mesh
lessons.objective: predict what each topology loses when one cable or device fails, count the cables and ports a mesh needs, and say which topology today's Ethernet actually uses.

lessons.title: Transmission media, impairments, and LPWAN
lessons.objective: classify guided and unguided media, explain attenuation, distortion and noise with decibels, and place LPWAN and IoT on the range and data-rate map.

lessons.title: Week 3 checkpoint
lessons.objective: answer exam-style questions on network classification, topologies, media and LPWAN without notes.

modules.title: The application layer
modules.outline: Principles and protocols: HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, peer-to-peer applications. Socket programming concepts. Lectures 08 to 10.

lessons.title: How applications talk: architectures, sockets, transport services
lessons.objective: compare client-server and P2P, explain how a socket and IP:port address a process, and choose TCP or UDP from an app's needs.

lessons.title: HTTP and the 2RTT rule
lessons.objective: read HTTP requests and responses, and compute page load time for non-persistent, parallel, persistent and pipelined connections.

lessons.title: Cookies, web caches, and conditional GET
lessons.objective: explain how a stateless protocol keeps state, compute what a cache does to access-link load, and trace a 304 Not Modified.

lessons.title: FTP and email: SMTP, POP3, IMAP
lessons.objective: describe FTP's two connections, trace an email from sender to reader, and say which protocol pushes and which pulls.

lessons.title: DNS: a distributed, hierarchical database
lessons.objective: draw the DNS hierarchy, walk an iterative resolution message by message, and read the four common record types.

lessons.title: Socket programming with UDP and TCP
lessons.objective: write the slides' uppercase client and server over UDP and over TCP, and explain the welcoming socket and the 4-tuple.

lessons.title: Week 4 checkpoint
lessons.objective: answer exam-style questions on the application layer without notes.

modules.title: The transport layer
modules.outline: Multiplexing and demultiplexing. TCP and UDP: connection-oriented versus connectionless protocols.

modules.title: The network layer: IP and routing
modules.outline: Network layer devices, the Internet Protocol, routing in the Internet.

modules.title: Addressing, subnetting, and wireless layer 3
modules.outline: Layer 3 wireless protocols for ad hoc and sensor networks. IP addressing and subnetting.

modules.title: The link layer: MAC, LLC, and virtualization
modules.outline: Introduction to the link layer, MAC and LLC sublayers, medium access techniques, link virtualization, data center networking.

modules.title: LLC protocols: ARP and RARP
modules.outline: Medium access control protocols and LLC protocols: ARP, RARP.

modules.title: Wireless and mobile networks
modules.outline: IEEE 802.11, cellular networks, mobile IP, IEEE 802.15.4 and IEEE 802.15.6.

modules.title: Multimedia networking
modules.outline: Streaming and stored video, voice over IP.

modules.title: Network management and the future
modules.outline: Infrastructure and the Internet standard management framework. Ubiquitous networks: AI and networks combined.
